French singer and cultural icon (born December 19, 1915, in Paris; died October 11, 1963, in Plascassier).

Best known for singing songs "[r=867885]", composed by [a=Louiguy], with lyrics by Piaf, and English lyrics adapted by [a=Mack David]; and "[url=http://www.discogs.com/Edith-Piaf-Non-Je-Ne-Regrette-Rien/master/266272]Non, Je Ne Regrette Rien[/url]" written by [a=Michel Vaucaire], which rather fittingly she sung just two years before the end of her eventful life.

In 1935 Piaf was discovered in the Pigalle area of Paris by nightclub owner [a=Louis Leplée], whose club Le Gerny off the Champs-Élysées was frequented by the upper and lower classes alike. He persuaded her to sing despite her extreme nervousness, which, combined with her height of only 142 centimetres (4 ft 8 in), inspired him to give her the nickname that would stay with her for the rest of her life and serve as her stage name, La Môme Piaf (Parigot translatable as "The Waif Sparrow", "The Little Sparrow", or "Kid Sparrow"). Leplée taught her the basics of stage presence and told her to wear a black dress, later to become her trademark apparel. Leplée ran an intense publicity campaign leading up to her opening night, attracting the presence of many celebrities, including actor [a=Maurice Chevalier]. Her nightclub gigs led to her first two records produced that same year, with one of them penned by [a=Marguerite Monnot], a collaborator throughout Piaf's life.

On 6 April 1936, Leplée was murdered, and Piaf was questioned and accused as an accessory but was acquitted. Leplée had been killed by mobsters with previous ties to Piaf. A barrage of negative media attention now threatened her career. To rehabilitate her image, she recruited [a=Raymond Asso], with whom she would become romantically involved. He changed her stage name to "Édith Piaf", barred undesirable acquaintances from seeing her, and commissioned Monnot to write songs that reflected or alluded to Piaf's previous life on the streets.

In 1940, Édith co-starred in [a=Jean Cocteau]'s successful one-act play "Le Bel Indifférent". She began forming friendships with prominent people, including Chevalier and poet Jacques Borgeat. She wrote the lyrics of many of her songs and collaborated with composers on the tunes. In 1944, she discovered [a=Yves Montand] in Paris, made him part of her act, and became his mentor and lover. Within a year, he became one of the most famous singers in France, and she broke off their relationship when he had become almost as popular as she was.

During this time, she was in great demand and very successful in Paris as France's most popular entertainer. After the war, she became known internationally, touring Europe, the United States, and South America. In Paris, she gave [a=Atahualpa Yupanqui] (Héctor Roberto Chavero) - the most important Argentine musician of folklore - the opportunity to share the scene, making his debut in July 1950. She helped launch the career of [a=Charles Aznavour] in the early 1950s, taking him on tour with her in France and the United States and recording some of his songs. At first, she met with little success with U.S. audiences, who regarded her as downcast. After a glowing review by a prominent New York critic, however, her popularity grew, to the point where she eventually appeared on The [a=Ed Sullivan] Show eight times and at Carnegie Hall twice (1956 and 1957).

Édith Piaf's signature song "La Vie En Rose" was written in 1945 and was voted a Grammy Hall of Fame Award in 1998.

[a=Bruno Coquatrix]'s famous Paris Olympia music hall is where Piaf achieved lasting fame, giving several series of concerts at the hall, the most famous venue in Paris, between January 1955 and October 1962. Excerpts from five of these concerts (1955, 1956, 1958, 1961, 1962) were issued on record and CD and have never been out of print. The 1961 concerts were promised by Piaf in an effort to save the venue from bankruptcy and where she debuted her song "Non, je ne regrette rien". In April 1963, Piaf recorded her last song, "L'Homme De Berlin".

She was married to [a=Jacques Pills] between 1952 and 1956, and to [a=Théo Sarapo] from 1962 until her death in 1963.

profile.profile: British rapper from Stockwell, South London, born 9 September 1972, London, England.

The Foreign Exchange is a musical duo consisting of American rapper/singer [a=Phonte] aka [a=Phonte Coleman] and Dutch producer/multi-instrumentalist [a=Nicolay] aka [a=Matthijs Rook]. Formed in 2002, the collaboration began when Phonte and Nicolay connected via the Okayplayer.com message boards and started exchanging music files online, despite never having met in person at the time. This long-distance partnership led to the release of their debut album, Connected, in 2004. Their subsequent albums include Leave It All Behind (2008), which featured the Grammy-nominated track "Daykeeper," Authenticity (2010), Love in Flying Colors (2013), and Tales from the Land of Milk and Honey (2015). The duo's music blends elements of hip-hop, R&B, soul, and electronica, characterized by introspective lyrics and sophisticated production. In addition to their work as a duo, Phonte and Nicolay founded the independent label [l=The Foreign Exchange Music], through which they have released their own projects as well as works by affiliated artists such as Zo!, Sy Smith, and Darien Brockington.

Legendary Memphis, Tennessee rockabilly and soul label founded by [a=Ray Harris (3)] (co-owner, 1957-1970), record store owner [a=Joe Cuoghi] (whose surname inspired the label name), former [l=Sun Records] staff producers [a=Bill Cantrell] and [a689215] and a trio of silent partners including Cuoghi's lawyer [a=Nick Pesce] in 1957.

Among its artists were [a=Willie Mitchell] (who was also a co-owner of the label from 1970-77), [a=Syl Johnson], [a=Jumpin' Gene Simmons], [a=Ann Peebles], [a=Bill Black's Combo], [a=O.V. Wright], the original Ebony Web [a=Michael Allen (2)] and, most famously, [a=Al Green].

Hi was distributed by [l=London Records] starting in 1959 with [m1826640] until the company's sale to Al Bennett's [l=Cream Records (4)] in 1977. The label became dormant in the early 1980s and licensed its catalog to [l=Motown] only to discover that it only reissued the Al Green material and left the rest of the catalog in the vaults (which violated the licensing agreement) plus the company faced copyright liens against its entire catalog placed by both Motown and Cream Records' creditors. Adelah Bennett Shaw, Bennett's daughter, fought this action and won eventually settling with its creditors and regaining the rights to the Hi catalog from Motown.

Shaw took over from her father after his death in 1989. She struck a new licensing agreement with Capitol-EMI's [l=The Right Stuff] reissue unit and reissued a number of albums from the Hi catalog on CD. Hi also was reactivated as an active label in the late 1990s, signing new acts and releasing new material.

Adelah Bennett Shaw died in 2008. The label is now distributed by  [l=Fat Possum Records] in North America and Australia and by [l=Demon Music Group] in Europe.

Label name also appears as "Hi" only.
